newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudan battlefield widens to Uganda border.
newsitem.headline: Sudan battlefield widens to Uganda border.

text.p: Sudan said on Sunday it had attacked a rebel base near the southern border with Uganda, opening another front in the war against rebels trying to overthrow the Islamist government.

State television quoted Information Minister Brigadier Al-Tayeb Ibrahim Mohamed Khair as saying the armed forces had killed several rebels and routed others in fighting which took place at Lokia, an area near the southern town of Torit about 75 km (47 miles) from the Uganda border.

"Several rebels were killed and wounded and a big number of heavy and light guns was seized," he said without giving any exact figures. "The rebels were chased away and the armed forces sustained a few wounded."
It was the first report of clashes so far south since the government's conflict with rebels began earlier this month.
There have been no independent accounts of the fighting in Sudan and it is difficult to assess the veracity of reports issued by the two sides.
Rebels and the government have previously reported clashes further to the north near the Ethiopian and Eritrean borders.
A Sudanese official was quoted on Sunday as saying government troops had killed opposition fighters in the east.
The official Sudan News Agency quoted Ali Maget, the head of Roseires town which is the site of a strategic dam, as saying the clash took place just south of the town in Um Darfa.

"The armed forces responded decisively to an attack launched by the Tigrean (Ethiopian) forces and the attack (on the Ethiopians) killed a big number of the attackers, forcing the rest to flee into Ethiopia," Maget said.
"The blow which the minority Tigrean forces faced have made them retreat into a narrow border strip where they are now besieged," he added.
Sudan says hostile neighbours Eritrea and Ethiopia are fighting with rebels seeking to pressure the government and spark a popular uprising -- the way previous governments have fallen in the past.
Both states deny any part in the fighting.
Khartoum has also said it expected a third front to open on the Uganda border but Sudan's President Omar Hassan al-Bashir said his troops would not move unless Uganda attacked first.

The rebels say their aim is to take the key southeastern town of Damazin, which the government is using as the pivot of its counterattack. A Sudanese government-owned daily said the state had sent 3,000 more volunteer troops to the southeast.
Damazin is near the strategic Roseires Dam which provides Khartoum with most of its electricity and the rebels say they are only a few kilometres away, a claim which Sudan denies.

The government has also scoffed at rebel reports that they have seized large chunks of land in the eastern Blue Nile state, admitting only to the loss of the small border towns of Kurmuk and Qeissan early in the conflict.
But Brigadier Khair was quoted on Sunday as saying the Ethiopians had captured six small towns in the Blue Nile state and destroyed their infrastructure, displacing about 30,000 people.
The government-owned al-Sudan al-Hadith quoted Khair as saying the Ethiopians had also abducted 4,000 people and that they had killed and "shamefully" treated them.
